review.headline: A Scotch Gambit that went wrong when you lost your queen on move 13

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4. After 5.Nxd4?! Nxd4 6.Qxd4 you had a safe, equal position, and Black replied with 6...c6?, which was inaccurate because 6...Bd6 was better.
7.O-O?! was fine, and 7...d5 attacked the centre. Then 8.Be2?? was the first blunder, because 8.exd5 would have kept you ahead. After 8...dxe4 you were behind.
10.f3?? was a second mistake: the best move was 10.Bf4. After 10...exf3 11.Bxf3 Bd6, White was under pressure and the queen was exposed.
Finally, 13.Qg3?? walked into 13...Bxg3, winning your queen. 13.Nc3 was the move that kept you in the game.

review.turning_point: 13.Qg3?? put the queen where the bishop on d6 could capture it.
review.focus: On move 8, 8.Be2 missed 8.exd5. When your opponent challenges the centre, take the pawn first and ask if the opponent has a recapture.

review.headline: A Petrov that stayed level until one pawn move cost a piece

sections.text: You went into the Petrov and traded queens early with 5...Qe7 and 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. That is a very safe line, and you reached a balanced endgame with equal chances.
You developed with 8...c6 and 9...Bg4, and 10...Bxf3 11.gxf3 wrecked White's pawns. Then 11...Nbd7 and 12...O-O were a sensible plan.
13.Bh6 Nh5 14.Be2 Rfe8?! was a slightly loose move, and then White played 15.f4, attacking the knight on h5. You replied with 15...g6??, which dropped it.
After 16.Bxh5 you were down material and resigned. 15...Ndf6 was the right way to keep the knight protected.

review.turning_point: 15...g6?? left the knight on h5 loose, and 16.Bxh5 won it.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn like 15...g6, ask which piece it leaves undefended. The knight on h5 had no support after that move.

review.headline: A wild Petrov Three Knights game with plenty of errors on both sides, decided on the clock

sections.text: You played the Three Knights Petrov and put the bishop on e6 with 4...Be6?! after 4.g3. After 7...c6? and 8.Ne2? both sides had made inaccuracies, but 10.c3?? from White really helped you, because 10.Nxe6 would have forked the queen and the rook.
You chose 9...Nbd7??, which allowed that line, but White did not take it. After 10...Bc4 and 11...Ne5 you were comfortable.
The middlegame turned on 15.Nxe7+? Qxe7!, which was the right recapture, and after 19.Qxd2 Rxd2 you had a nice endgame with the rook on the seventh. Then 23...g4! was a strong reply to 23.a4?.

You got a little loose with 28...Nxe4? and 29...Nxc3?, and 40.Bc6+?? was a discovered check from White that gave you a chance. After 40...Kd6?, 42...Ke6?? and 43...Nc6??, the position was bad for you, but you won on time after 43 moves.

review.turning_point: 15...Qxe7! equalised after 15.Nxe7+?, and the endgame later turned wild with mistakes on both sides.
review.focus: In the endgame 40...Kd6? and 42...Ke6?? gave up the edge. Try to calculate king moves carefully when checks are around.

review.headline: A Petrov where you outplayed your opponent after a knight misstep and converted with pressure on the a-file

sections.text: You played the Petrov and accepted a queen trade early, with 7...Qe7?! 8.Qxe7+ Bxe7. The position stayed level, and you developed with 9...O-O and 10...Re8.
You captured with 12...cxd4 and then 13...Nbd7?!, and 14...Rd8?? weakened the position, where 14...Bd8 was safer. But your opponent replied with 15.Nd6??, which is a blunder.
You found 15...Bxd6!, winning a knight, and from there it was a clear plus. White's 22.Be3? let you play 22...Ra5!, and 23...Rxa7 won the pawn on a7 with an edge.
You closed the game with 25...Bxb4! and 26...Bxc3, then 27...Bxa1, picking up pawns and the rook on a1 with your bishop. A pleasant, technical win.

review.turning_point: 15...Bxd6! punished 15.Nd6?? by taking a knight outright and set up the whole conversion.
review.focus: Look at 14...Rd8?? again: 14...Bd8 was the safe move and avoided any risk. Check your pieces' defenders before choosing a rook move.
